threads.thread_goal: Align on overall click-and-collect process and role responsibilities.

messages.text:
Kicking off the Retail Click-and-Collect Service Rollout channel.
I have a first draft of the end-to-end process for T1 mapped out and plugged into the outline for A1.
High level flow I am proposing:
1) Order intake and payment: office clerk logs the order using existing tools, confirms payment via current POS, and adds it to the tracking sheet.
2) Staging request: office clerk notifies sales assistant and, when needed, mover for bulky or fragile items.
3) In-store staging and storage: sales assistant prepares the order, coordinates with specialised sellers when needed, and uses the staging checklist.
4) Movement of bulky or sensitive items: mover brings items to the staging area following the handling rules.
5) Pickup and confirmation: customer arrives at pickup point, sales assistant hands over the order, office clerk updates status and closes the order.
Before I lock this into A1, can you all review the responsibilities and flag anything missing or unclear in T1?

Thanks for laying this out.
From the sales floor side, the steps make sense.
One thing I want to clarify: when you say sales assistant prepares the order, I am assuming that includes checking stock, picking items, labeling, and placing them in the staging area.
For mixed baskets (for example, regular goods plus bakery or garden items), do you see the specialised sellers preparing their part and then handing it to the sales assistant, or do they keep responsibility until pickup?

On the garden side, I would prefer that we keep plants in our area until shortly before pickup, especially for orders with specific light or watering needs.
Maybe the specialised seller prepares and tags the plant, but the final move to the pickup point is coordinated with the sales assistant.
That way we can follow the floral and garden staging instructions that will go into A4 and still fit into the general flow in A1.

From the moving side, I see my part mainly in steps 3 and 4.
I would get a list of orders that need help because they are bulky or fragile, then bring them from storage to the staging area.
I want to be sure we write down clearly when I get involved.
Is it only when the item is too heavy or big for the sales assistant, or also when it is fragile like electronics or glass?

For electronics, I would lean toward involving you whenever the box is large or there is a risk of dropping it on the way to staging or pickup.
We can align that with the handling rules in A3.
Maybe we define a simple rule in T3 and T1, like: mover supports any item above a certain size or weight, plus specific categories such as TVs and sound systems.

On mixed baskets, my proposal is:
- Specialised sellers prepare and tag their own sensitive items (bakery, floral, electronics) and keep them in their optimal area.
- Sales assistant remains the single point of contact for the full order and coordinates with you.
- Shortly before pickup, mover or sales assistant brings everything to the pickup point.
I will reflect that in T1 and A1 as: sales assistant owns the full order, specialised sellers own product-specific prep until final move.

That works for me.
For the pickup step, I suggest we keep it simple at the counter: sales assistant checks ID or order number, confirms items, and hands over.
But someone needs to be clearly responsible for updating the tracking sheet and sending the final confirmation to the customer.
I would rather that sit with office clerks, since they already manage A2 and the communication templates in A5.

I can take on the final update in the tracking sheet and trigger the ready or picked-up status using A2.
For the customer-facing confirmation, we will have templates in A5 as part of T4.
So the flow at pickup would be: sales assistant completes the handover, then office clerk marks the order as picked up and sends the confirmation if needed.
This keeps the data and messages consistent.

I am ok with a simple rule for when I step in.
Maybe we can list the product types in A3 and then just reference that list in A1 and T1.
That way I know that if the order includes any of those items, I should plan a run to move them to staging before the pickup window.

One more detail from the garden side: for plants that cannot stay long in low light, I suggest we add a note in A1 that they should be moved to the pickup point as late as possible.
The sales assistant can still be the main contact, but we should write down that they check with us on timing for those orders.
I will also reflect this in T6 so it stays aligned.

Let me summarise the high-level flow for T1 and A1 based on this thread:
- Office clerk: logs order, confirms payment, maintains A2, and sends customer messages using A5.
- Sales assistant: coordinates picking, staging, and handover at pickup point, including mixed baskets.
- Specialised sellers: prepare and care for sensitive items (bakery, floral, electronics) until final move.
- Mover: moves bulky or fragile items according to A3 and supports final staging.
If no one objects, I will treat this as the approved end-to-end flow for the rollout.

The summary matches what I had in mind.
On the question of who is responsible for final pickup confirmation to customers, I support the idea that office clerks own that step, using the templates in A5.
Sales assistants will focus on the in-person handover and making sure the order is complete and correctly staged.

Agreed.
I will take responsibility, as office clerk, for the final pickup confirmation to customers.
That means updating A2 to the picked-up status and sending the confirmation message from A5.
We can document this clearly in T1 so there is no confusion at the counter.

The flow looks clear from my side.
Once you lock this into A1 and T1, please share the final version so I can check that the timing of my runs fits with the daily route planning in T9.
I want to avoid blocking the aisles during busy hours when I move bulky orders to staging.

I am fine with this structure.
Just a small ask: when you write A1, can you add a short note that floral and garden items may stay in our area until shortly before pickup, as we discussed.
That will help our team follow T6 without guessing.

Perfect, thanks everyone.
I will update T1 and A1 today with the agreed responsibilities and the rule that office clerks handle final pickup confirmation using A2 and A5.
Once done, I will share the updated A1 so you can all use it as the reference for your own tasks.

Once your updated A1 is out, I will align the detailed steps in T4, T5, T8, and T12 so that all office workflows match the approved flow.
I will also make sure the status codes in A2 reflect the pickup confirmation step clearly.

From the sales floor side, I will start sketching how the staging and pickup counter routine fits into this flow so that T2, T7, and T11 stay consistent with A1.
I will share a draft later for feedback.

threads.thread_goal: Define practical staging, storage, and handling rules for different product types.

messages.text:
Following up on the overall flow, here is an initial proposal for labeling and storage for staged orders for T2.
Label format:
- Order ID
- Customer name (initial plus last name)
- Pickup date and time window
- Number of packages (for example, 1 of 3)
- Special handling icons (fragile, chilled, plants)
Storage zoning:
- Zone A: standard goods
- Zone B: fragile and electronics
- Zone C: bulky items staged by movers
- Zone D: short-stay area near floral and bakery for sensitive items
This would be documented in A8 and referenced in A1.
Can you check if these zones and label fields work from your sides?

From the moving side, having a dedicated Zone C for bulky items is helpful.
I would like to add that Zone C should be close to an entrance or a wide aisle so I can bring items in without blocking customers.
For the labels, could we add a simple code that tells me if I need to use a trolley or two-person lift, or is that too detailed for T3?

For documentation, I like that the label mirrors the fields in A2.
If we keep the order ID and customer name consistent between A2 and the physical label, it will be easier to find orders.
I suggest we standardise the special handling icons based on A3 and A4, so we do not invent new symbols in each department.

Zone D for sensitive items works, but for plants I would like to keep them in our area until close to pickup, as we said.
Maybe we can say that Zone D is a virtual zone for floral and bakery, meaning the label is prepared and the order is marked as staged in A2, but the physical item stays with us until the last moment.
In T6 and A4 I can describe how we handle watering and light while they wait.

From the office side, the label fields you propose line up well with what we plan in A2 for T5.
I would only add a small barcode or QR code field if we can generate it from existing tools, but since we cannot buy new software, we might need to keep it manual for now.
So I support your current label fields as the base standard.

Good point on the lift support.
To keep the label readable, how about we add a simple code like B for bulky and H for heavy, based on the handling rules in A3.
We can define those codes in T3 and list them in A8 so everyone understands them.
That way you know when to bring a trolley without overloading the label.

Yes, a simple B or H code is enough for me.
If we write in A3 that B means bulky and H means heavy, I will know what equipment to use.
Please also note in T2 that Zone C should have enough space for trolleys to turn.

For plants, I will define in T6 that we tag them with the same label format but keep them on our benches.
When the pickup window starts, we move them to the pickup point or Zone D.
In A4 I will also add icons for sun, shade, and fragile stems so movers and sales assistants know how to handle them.

On fragile and electronics in Zone B, I will make sure A3 includes clear packaging instructions, especially for TVs and audio equipment.
We should also note in A8 that Zone B shelves should not be overloaded and that boxes are stacked only up to a safe height.
This will help prevent damage before pickup.

Given our constraint on tools, I agree we keep the label manual for now.
I will align the fields in A2 so that order ID, customer name, pickup window, and special handling codes match exactly what you print on the label.
This will also make it easier to use A7 later when we log and resolve issues.

Let me recap the labeling and zoning approach so we can lock it in for T2 and A8:
- Label fields: order ID, customer name (initial plus last name), pickup date and time window, package count, and special handling icons.
- Codes: B for bulky, H for heavy, plus icons for fragile, chilled, and plants, aligned with A3 and A4.
- Zones: A for standard goods, B for fragile and electronics, C for bulky items, D as a short-stay or virtual zone for floral and bakery.
If everyone is ok with this, I will treat it as our standard labeling and storage zoning approach.

The recap matches what I need.
With Zones B and C clearly defined, I can plan my route in T9 so that I move bulky and fragile items at set times.
Please just make sure A3 lists the B and H codes so I do not miss them on the labels.

I am aligned with this.
In T6 and A4 I will describe how we keep plants in our area until pickup and then move them to Zone D.
I will also use the same icons you mentioned so the labels are consistent.

From the office side, I confirm that this labeling and zoning scheme works and I will reference it in A1 and A7 when we describe how to find and escalate issues with staged orders.
It will also help when we train staff using A6 and A8.

With this agreed, I will make sure the handling rules in A3 and the staging checklist in A8 reference Zones A to D and the B and H codes.
This will also feed into the training checklist in T7 so everyone learns the same pattern.
On handling rules for fragile, bulky, and perishable items, I suggest we confirm that A3 and A4 will be our final reference for launch.

I confirm that for movers we will follow A3 as the main reference for handling fragile, bulky, and perishable items.
Once you and the specialised sellers finalise A3 and A4, I will adjust my daily routine in T9 to match those rules.

From the floral and garden side, I agree that A4, aligned with A3, will be our final rule set for handling plants and similar items.
I will make sure T6 is consistent with that and with the zones we defined.

Then we can state that A3 and A4, together with A8, are our final handling rules for fragile, bulky, and perishable items for launch.
I will update T2 to reference them explicitly so that the staging and labeling method is fully aligned.

Great, I will cross-check A1 so that it points to A3, A4, and A8 for any handling questions.
This will also feed into A6 when we prepare the training sessions.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize order tracking and documentation workflow for office clerks.

messages.text:
I have a first draft of the order tracking sheet for T5 and the filing rules for T12 ready to review.
For A2, the sheet currently has these fields:
- Order ID
- Customer name
- Contact details
- Items summary
- Status (New, In preparation, Staged, Ready for pickup, Picked up, Cancelled, Returned)
- Pickup deadline
- Storage zone (A, B, C, D)
- Notes (for example, B or H code, special handling)
For T12, I propose we keep paper documents in a click-and-collect binder by date and store digital copies in a shared folder with subfolders by month.
Can you check if these fields and the status codes cover your needs?

Thanks for sharing.
From my side, the status list looks good and matches the flow we agreed in A1.
I would add one more status: Delayed, so we can track when we have informed the customer using A5.
For T12, we should also define a simple naming convention for digital files, maybe order ID plus date, to make retrieval easier.

From the sales floor, the key for us is being able to quickly see if an order is staged and where it is.
The Storage zone field and the Status field already cover that.
Could we also have a simple flag or note when an order includes plants or bakery goods, so we know to coordinate with specialised sellers before promising a pickup time at the counter?

Yes, a flag for plants would help.
Maybe we can use the same icons we defined for labels in A4 and A8 and just note them in the Notes field.
In T6 I can specify that when the plant icon is present, the sales assistant should check with us before confirming exact pickup time.

For movers, I mainly need to see which orders are in Zone C or have B or H codes.
If the Storage zone and Notes fields show that, I can plan my runs.
Maybe we can also add a simple time field for when the order should be moved to staging, so I do not move bulky items too early.

Good call on the Delayed status.
I will add it between Ready for pickup and Cancelled.
For T12, I like the idea of using order ID plus date as the file name.
So a digital file could be something like CC-OrderID-Date, stored in a monthly folder.
We can test retrieval of three sample orders as required in T12.

On the time field for movers, we could add a column called Move by, which indicates the latest time the order should be in the staging area.
This would be filled by the office clerk when confirming the pickup window with the customer using A5.
That way your T9 planning can rely on A2 without extra messages.

If we use the same icons in the Notes field, that should be enough for us.
When I see the plant or bakery icon, I will check with the specialised seller before confirming a tight pickup window.
We can also include this in A7 as a common issue prevention tip.

Let me summarise the final field list for A2 and T5:
- Order ID
- Customer name
- Contact details
- Items summary
- Status (New, In preparation, Staged, Ready for pickup, Delayed, Picked up, Cancelled, Returned)
- Pickup deadline
- Move by time
- Storage zone (A, B, C, D)
- Notes (B or H codes, plant or bakery icons, other remarks)
If everyone agrees, I will treat this as the approved structure and start testing with five mock orders.

This list works for me.
With the Move by time and Storage zone, I can plan my daily route in T9.
Please share the mock sheet once you have tested it so I can try a day of moves on paper.

I am fine with this structure.
The Notes field will be enough for us to mark plant-related details.
In T6 and A4 I will just make sure we describe how to use those icons consistently.

From the sales floor, this setup will help us quickly check if an order is ready and where it is.
Please include a short explanation of the statuses and icons in A7 so new staff can look it up during busy times.

On T12, we still need to confirm the archiving rules.
I propose:
- Paper: keep in a daily binder for 1 month at the counter, then move to monthly archive boxes for 12 months.
- Digital: store in a shared click-and-collect folder, with subfolders by year and month, and keep for at least 2 years.
This should cover basic receipt retention without overloading storage.
If we agree, we can document this in A1 and A7 as the standard.

Your proposal sounds reasonable and fits with what we do for other documents.
I will check with store management to confirm that the 12-month paper and 2-year digital retention meets our compliance expectations.
Assuming they agree, I will write this into T12 and update A2 and A7 to reference the archive locations.

With the fields and statuses agreed and the archiving rules defined, we can say that A2 and T5 are approved for launch.
I will help you run the test with five mock orders to make sure there is no data loss and that retrieval works as described in T12.

threads.thread_goal: Align on customer communication templates and exception handling.

messages.text:
I have drafted the customer communication templates for T4 and the procedure for partial pickups, cancellations, and refunds for T8.
For A5, I prepared three main templates:
1) Order confirmation: includes order ID, items summary, expected pickup window, and what documents to bring.
2) Ready for pickup: confirms that the order is staged, where to go in the store, and the pickup deadline.
3) Delay or issue notice: explains the delay, new expected time, and who to contact.
For T8, the exception procedure follows our existing POS rules for refunds.
Can you review and suggest any changes before we ask store management to approve A5?

I reviewed your drafts.
The structure is clear.
I would suggest we add a short note in the order confirmation about how we handle mixed orders with perishable or fragile items, so customers know they should pick them up within a shorter window.
We can base that on A3 and A4.
For T8, we should also mention that any refund must be processed through the existing POS flow, not manually.

From the counter perspective, it would help if the ready-for-pickup template clearly states the pickup point location and any time limits.
That way we can just repeat the same message in person.
For partial pickups, we need a simple step-by-step in T8 so that sales assistants know when to call the office clerk and when they can handle it directly at the counter.

For movers, the main impact is when there is a delay or a partial pickup.
If the delay notice in A5 includes a new Move by time, that will help me adjust my route.
In T8, please also note that if a bulky item is cancelled after staging, I need to know whether to move it back to storage or to a returns area.

For floral and garden orders, I would like the confirmation and ready messages to mention that plants should be picked up as close as possible to the start of the window, not at the very end.
We can base that on A4.
If a customer cancels a plant order, T8 should say whether we return the plant to the sales floor or treat it as waste, depending on its condition.

I will update the ready-for-pickup template to include:
- Exact pickup point name and a short description (for example, near customer service desk).
- Pickup window and a clear deadline.
For T8, I propose this split:
- Sales assistant can handle partial pickups where the remaining items stay in the same order and no refund is needed.
- Office clerk handles any case with refunds or changes to payment, following POS rules.
We can document this in A7 as well.

I agree with that split.
I will help you write the T8 steps so that sales assistants have a clear decision tree: when there is no refund, they can proceed; when there is any money back or change in items, they call the office clerk.
We will also make sure A5 uses simple language so customers understand what happens in each case.

That decision tree will help a lot at the counter.
Please also include in A7 a short example for each scenario: partial pickup without refund, partial pickup with refund, full cancellation before staging, and cancellation after staging.
This will make it easier to train new staff using A6.

I have now updated the three templates in A5 to:
- Mention shorter pickup expectations for perishable and fragile items, referencing A3 and A4.
- Clarify that refunds are always processed through the existing POS.
- Include the pickup point location and required documents.
Unless there are strong objections, I suggest we move forward and ask store management to approve A5 for launch.

I support sending A5 for approval.
The templates now cover confirmation, ready, and delay scenarios clearly.
Once management signs off, we can lock T4 as done and share the templates with all staff.

On cancellations after staging, I suggest T8 says that bulky items go back to their original storage location unless they are damaged.
If damaged, we should follow the usual damage process and note it in A2 and A7.
Please also mention in the delay template that the new Move by time will be updated in A2 so I know when to move items again.

For plants, I agree that cancelled orders should usually go back to the sales floor if the plant is still in good condition.
If not, we follow our usual waste procedure.
We can add a short note in T8 and A4 so that staff know which option to choose.

Once T8 and A7 include those examples, I will incorporate them into the training checklist in A6 and T7.
That way, during training we can walk through each scenario and practice what to say to customers using A5.

Let me summarise the exception handling for T8 so we can confirm it:
- Partial pickup without refund: sales assistant hands over part of the order, updates A2 status and notes, remaining items stay staged.
- Partial pickup with refund: sales assistant calls office clerk, who processes refund via POS and updates A2.
- Full cancellation before staging: office clerk cancels in POS and A2, no movement needed.
- Cancellation after staging: mover returns bulky items to storage, specialised sellers decide on plants and bakery based on condition, and office clerk updates A2 and A7.
If this matches your understanding, we can treat it as the agreed process.

The summary is aligned with what we discussed.
I will finalise T8 with these steps and update A7 to include the examples and escalation paths.
Once store management approves A5, we can consider D7 and D8 closed for launch.

threads.thread_goal: Plan training, daily routines, and go-live readiness check.

messages.text:
With the main flows and templates shaping up, I have drafted the training checklist for T7 and a first idea for the go-live date.
For A6, the checklist has three sections:
1) Sales floor: order lookup in A2, staging using A8, handover at pickup point, basic troubleshooting using A7.
2) Office: order intake, tracking in A2, customer messages using A5, exception handling from T8.
3) Movers: daily route from T9, handling rules from A3 and A4, staging support in Zones B and C.
Given the 21-day deadline, I propose we target go-live in 14 days to leave a week for adjustments.
Thoughts?

The structure of A6 looks solid.
For the office section, I would add a short exercise where clerks process a mock order from New to Picked up in A2, including a delay scenario using A5.
On the go-live date, 14 days sounds ambitious but doable if we start training early next week.
We should also plan a readiness checklist review two days before go-live, as per our channel rituals.

I like the idea of a mock order exercise.
We can reuse the five test orders from T5 so that training also validates A2 and T12.
For exceptions, we should walk through at least one partial pickup and one cancellation using the steps in T8 and the messages in A5.

For movers, I would like the training to include a short walk of the route we plan in T9.
We can practice moving a bulky order from storage to Zone C and then to the pickup point, following A3.
It would also help to show where Zones B and C are physically so there is no confusion.

For floral and garden, I suggest we add to A6 a short block on how we stage plants according to A4 and T6.
We can show where we keep them before pickup and how we label them.
This will help sales assistants and movers understand why we sometimes keep plants in our area until the last moment.

I will add the mock order exercise for office clerks and the route walk for movers into A6.
For the go-live timeline, if we start training in 3 days, we can run short sessions over a week and still hit a go-live in 14 days.
We just need to make sure A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A7, and A8 are in near-final form before training starts.

On readiness, I propose we create a simple go-live checklist linked to A1 and A6, covering:
- A2 tracking sheet tested with mock orders.
- A5 templates approved by management.
- A3, A4, and A8 printed and available at relevant stations.
- At least one training session completed for each role.
We can review this checklist in a dedicated thread two days before go-live.

I can own that go-live checklist.
I will base it on A1 and A7 and share it here once A5 is approved.
During the readiness review, we can also check that T5 and T12 are fully in place so we do not miss any documentation steps.

For the mover training, I will prepare a simple route plan for T9 with time slots that avoid peak customer hours.
During the session, we can walk the route and adjust if we see any bottlenecks.
I will also bring examples of packaging materials we use, as described in A3.

I will prepare a short demo for the training showing how we label and store plants according to A4 and T6.
We can also show what happens if a plant is not picked up on time and how we decide whether to return it to the floor or not.

For sales assistants, I will design a short role-play for training where we:
- Look up an order in A2.
- Find it in the staging area using A8.
- Handle a simple issue using A7 and, if needed, call the office clerk.
This should make the new routine more concrete before go-live.

On the proposed go-live in 14 days, I suggest we tentatively book that date but keep a checkpoint after the first round of training.
If we see major gaps, we can still adjust by a couple of days while staying within the 21-day limit.
I will also prepare a short daily async check-in format so each role can post blockers on their T tasks.

For the async check-ins, we can base updates on A2 and A7: each role posts which orders or issues are blocked and what they need from others.
I will also send twice-weekly progress summaries using data from A2, as part of our rituals.

The 14-day target works for me as long as we confirm the route in T9 during training.
If we find that some aisles are too crowded, we might need to adjust time slots, but that should not block go-live.
I will share my draft route plan in the next couple of days.

From the garden side, the timeline is fine.
Our main dependency is having A4 and T6 finalised before we train.
I will aim to complete T6 in the next few days so we can include it in A6.

I will finalise A6 with all the inputs from this thread and share it for a quick review before we start training.
Once we have that and the go-live checklist from A1 and A7, we should be in a good position to hit the 14-day target.
